claims.text: Equiatomic multi-metal nanoparticles can initially be crystallized as a homogeneous, disordered single-phase solid solution.
Atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice strain predominantly governs retention of structural and chemical homogeneity from 473 K to 1923 K.
Minimal isovalent substitutions can change atomic size mismatch without significantly changing overall mixing entropy.
Increasing atomic size mismatch increases lattice strain, while decreasing the mismatch decreases lattice strain.
Lattice strain alters atomic diffusion barriers.
Atomic size mismatch and associated lattice effects influence local compositional ordering.
Higher lattice strain reduces effective diffusion barriers.
Reduced diffusion barriers caused by higher lattice strain promote local ordering or phase separation at lower temperatures.
Lower lattice strain helps preserve a disordered single-phase solid solution up to 1923 K.
Nanoparticles with intentionally increased lattice strain will exhibit phase separation or local compositional ordering at a lower onset temperature than low-strain baseline nanoparticles.
The onset of ordering or phase separation can be detected through diffraction changes and microstructural features.
Baseline nanoparticles with minimal lattice strain will remain a stable single-phase solid solution throughout 473–1923 K.
The prediction is conditioned on constant overall mixing entropy and the absence of oxidation or unintended compositional changes.
Local compositional fluctuations and measurement resolution may affect the measured shift in phase-separation onset temperature.
Failure of the increased-strain material to show a lower phase-separation or ordering onset than the baseline would falsify the proposed strain-control relationship.

contradictions.description: The design states that the two sets have identical overall compositions while also requiring elemental substitutions in the test group. Unless 'identical' refers only to total atom count or another explicitly defined constraint, substitution changes elemental composition.
